## Methods

Brain samples collection
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants recruited for this study or, where applicable, from their legal guardians prior to participation in this study. The protocol of human subjects was approved by the ethics committee of the University of Colorado and Children’s Hospital Colorado (COMIRBs #95–500).

Cell lines
The medulloblastoma cell line D425 was purchased from Millipore Sigma (SCC290). D458 was purchased from Cellosaurus (CVCL_1161), D283 from ATCC (HTB-185), and D341 from ATCC (HTB-187), respectively. MB002 was provided by Dr. Martine Roussel (St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital). HDMB03 was provided by Dr. Mahapatra of the University of Nebraska. Human astrocytes were cultured in complete Astrocyte Medium (ScienCell, 1801). MAF1433 cells were isolated and cultured from the primary tumor of a patient with G3-MB. The D425 and D458 cell lines were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% 1× penicillin/streptomycin solution, 1% 1× L-glutamine, and 1% sodium pyruvate. D283 cells were cultured in DMEM (Thermo Fisher) supplemented with 10% FBS, 1mM sodium pyruvate, 1× penicillin/streptomycin solution (Cellgro), and 1× nonessential amino acids (Millipore Sigma). HDMB03 cells were cultured in 90% RPMI 1640, 10% FBS, and 1× penicillin/streptomycin. D341 and MB002 were cultured in neurobasal medium (Sigma, SCM003) containing 2% B-27, 1μg/ml heparin, 2mM L-glutamine, 1% penicillin/streptomycin, 25ng/ml fibroblast growth factor (FGF), and 25ng/ml epidermal growth factor (EGF). All cell lines were cultured at 37°C in 95% air and 5% CO2. All cell lines tested negative for Mycoplasma. Cell proliferation assays and live-cell imaging were performed using an Incucyte SX5 Live-Cell Analysis System (Sartorius). All cell lines are periodically authenticated by DNA fingerprinting, and we will continue to fingerprint all cell lines every 6 months.

Transfection
shRNA vectors targeting CDK8 mRNA (TRCN0000350344 and TRCN0000382350) and a non-targeting control shRNA were obtained from the Functional Genomics Facility at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. TRCN0000350344 was used for bulk RNA sequencing, CUT&RUN, and animal studies. The human MYC (NM_002467.6) expression construct was purchased from VectorBuilder (VB010000-9492agg). shRNAs targeting c-MYC were also obtained from VectorBuilder: shRNA #1 (VB241123-1086vdf), shRNA #2 (VB241123-1087jkp), and shRNA #3 (VB241123-1088rds). The corresponding vector control was VB010000-9526zpu. Viral transduction was performed as described previously33,43.

Methylcellulose assay
2000 cells/3 mL were plated in a 1:1 mixture of 2.6% methylcellulose and complete growth medium. The cells were allowed to grow for two weeks. Colonies were stained with nitrotetrazolium blue chloride (Sigma) at 1.5 mg/mL in PBS for 24 h at 37°C and counted.

Aldehyde dehydrogenase assay
ALDH activity was measured using an Aldefluor kit (Stem Cell Technologies), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, 1× 105 cells were resuspended in 0.5 mL Aldefluor buffer, separated equally into two tubes, and 5 μl of DEAB reagent was added to one tube as a negative control. Then 1.25 μl of Aldefluor Reagent was added to each tube and mixed well. After incubation at 37°C for 45 min and centrifugation, the cells were stained with propidium iodide and analyzed using a FlowSight Imaging Flow Cytometer (EMD Millipore).

Neurosphere assay
Medulloblastoma cells were grown for 14 days in neurosphere medium. The spheres were disassociated and replanted into 100-, 10-, and single-cell suspensions on day 14. The cells were grown for an additional 14 days with or without RVU120. The spheres were imaged using an Incucyte S3 Live Cell Imaging System (Sartorius).

Immunofluorescence
The cells were washed and seeded onto polylysine-coated slides, and then fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at room temperature, permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100 in PBS for 15 min, and incubated in 3% BSA diluted in 0.05% Triton X-100 for 30 min at room temperature on a shaker. After blocking, the cells were incubated with the primary antibodies. The following antibodies were used: phospho-4EBP1 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-293124, 1:50), CDK8 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-13155, 1:50), CDK8 (Abcam, ab224828, 1:200), CDK8 (Invitrogen, PA5-11500, 1:200), fibrillarin (Abcam, EPR10823, 1:200), nucleolin (Abcam, EPR7952, 1:200), and ribosomal RNA antibody Y10B (Abcam, ab171119, 1:200) for 1 h at room temperature. After washing with 0.05% Triton X-100, cells were incubated with Alexa Fluor 647- or Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody (1:500) for 1 hour at room temperature in the dark, washed with PBS, and mounted using ProLong Gold antifade reagent containing DAPI (Sigma). Images were acquired using an inverted epifluorescence microscope at × magnification of 40x.

Western blotting
Western blotting was performed as described previously32. Antibodies used for western blot analysis were from the following sources: β-actin (Cell Signaling, 8457, 1:2000), CDK8 (Cell Signaling, 4101, 1:1000), 4EBP1 (Cell Signaling, 9644S, 1:1000), phospho-4EBP1 (Cell Signaling, 2855S, 1:1000), STAT1 (Cell Signaling, 9176S, 1:1000), phospho-STAT1 (Cell Signaling, 8826S, 1:1000), S6 (Cell Signaling, 2217T, 1:1000), phospho-S6 (Cell Signaling, 4858T, 1:1000), RNA Pol II (Cell Signaling, 2629S, 1:1000), and phospho-RNA Pol II-Ser2 (Cell Signaling, 13499, 1:1000).

CDK8 and mTOR inhibitors
The CDK8 inhibitors RVU120, Torin1, and TAK-228 were purchased from MedChemExpress, and RVU120 for animal studies was provided by Ryvu Therapeutics. The drugs were reconstituted in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). An equivalent amount of DMSO at the highest concentration of the drug was used for each experiment as a vehicle control.

Extreme limiting dilution assay
The cells were treated with the indicated concentrations of RVU120 and then seeded into 96-well ultra-low-attachment plates in neurosphere media at increasing concentrations from 1 to 250 cells/well. Cells were seeded from n=5 wells (250 cells/well, 100 cells/well), n=10 wells (10–50 cells/well), or n=30 wells (1 cell/well) per condition. The cells were allowed to grow for 14 days, and the number of wells containing neurospheres was counted under a microscope.

Protein synthesis assay
The MB cells were plated at a density of 2000 cells/well in a 96-well plate and cultured overnight. The next day, the cells were treated with either vehicle or RVU120 for 1, 24, or 48 h. The cells were then collected and centrifuged at 400 × g and resuspended in OPP (O-propargyl-puromycin) working solution (Cayman Chemical, 601100). The mixed cells were incubated for 30 min at 37°C for OPP labeling of translated peptides. Following incubation, cells were fixed, washed, and analyzed using flow cytometry.

Drug interaction assay
Medulloblastoma cells were plated in 96-well low-attachment plates and subjected to dose-response assessments for individual drugs, as well as various concentrations of drug combinations, with DMSO (0.1%) and media serving as controls. The growth inhibition was quantified using the Cell Titer 96 AQueous Non-Radioactive Cell Proliferation Assay (Promega) and the Incucyte SX5 Live-Cell Analysis System (Sartorius). At least five independent trials were conducted to ensure reproducibility of the results. The Chou-Talalay median-effect model and the Bliss independence dose-response surface model were used to classify whether the two drugs interacted in an antagonistic, additive, or synergistic manner. For the Chou-Talalay median-effect model, CI > 1 indicated antagonism, CI = 1 demonstrated activity, and CI < 1 indicated synergistic interactions.

Unbound brain-to-plasma partition coefficient (Kpuu)
RVU120 was given to animals as a single dose of 10mg/kg by an intravenous (rats, due to limited bioavailability in rats) and oral (mice) administration. At predefined time points (4 h for mice, 2 h for rats) animals were anesthetized and blood samples were collected by heart puncture using a heparinized syringe and centrifuged at 4°C and 4000 × g for 5 min to obtain plasma. Immediately after the final blood sample was obtained, the lumbar CSF c was ollected by a single lumbar puncture. Plasma CSF samples were stored at −20°C until use.
The quantification of RVU120 in plasma and CSF samples was performed using liquid chromatography – tandem mass spectrometry method (LC/MS/MS). Briefly, the proteins in the samples (55 µL of plasma or 10 µL of CSF) were precipitated with 200 uL acetonitrile and, centrifugated at 4°C and 10,000g for 15 min and the supernatants were injected on LC/MS/MS. Compound was analyzed in multiple reaction monitoring (MRN) mode using a Sciex QTrap 5500 instrument (Torrance, MA, USA) equipped with Shimadzu DGU-20A5R(C) LC system (Kyoto, Japan) with Phenomenex Kinetex C18, 2.6 µ 100A, 30*2.1 mm; (Torrance, CA, USA) as analytical chromatography column.
The unbound fraction of compound in murine and rat plasma was determined by equilibrium dialysis with Rapid Equilibrium Dialysis (RED) Device (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Rockford, IL, USA). Plasma samples were spiked with the test compound (1 or 5 µM) and were dialyzed versus buffer (150 mM sodium phosphate buffer). The 96-well equilibrium dialysis apparatus was maintained on a rotator (set at 100 rpm) in an incubator at 37°C for 18 h. Samples, after unifying the matrix and protein precipitation, were vortexed and centrifuged for 20 minutes at 4°C at 2000g. The supernatants were then transferred into the HPLC plate for LC-MS analysis.
CSF-to-plasma unbound concentration ratios (Kp,uu) were calculated as follows:
Kp,uu = C_CSF / (C_p * f_p) (1)
Where C_CSF, C_p, f_p represent respectively CSF concentration, plasma concentration and the unbound fraction in plasma.

RNA-seq
RNA was isolated from cells under the indicated experimental conditions using a Qiagen miRNeasy kit (Valencia) and measured using an Agilent Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies). Illumina Novaseq 6000 libraries were prepared and sequenced by Novogene (CA, USA) or the Genomics and Microarray Core Facility at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. High-quality base calls at Q30 ≥ 80% were obtained with approximately 40M paired paired-end reads. Sequenced 150bp pair-end reads were mapped to the human genome (GRCh38) by STAR (v2.4.0.1), read counts were calculated by R Bioconductor package GenomicAlignments (v1.18.1), and differential expression was analyzed with DESeq2 (v1.22.2) in R. Further analysis by GSEA was performed using GSEA (v2.1.0) software with 1000 data permutations and Cytoscape (v3.10.1).

Gene set enrichment analysis
Gene sets from MSigDB were downloaded and used to estimate biological activity. The ssGSEA algorithm in the R package GSVA (v.1.40.1) was applied to estimate signature enrichment in the bulk transcript datasets. The enrichment results of GO and pathways among differentially expressed genes were generated using the R package clusterProfiler (v.4.7.1).

CUT&RUN
A total of 500,000 cells per reaction were harvested and captured using 10 µL of pre-activated ConA beads (EpiCypher). Beads with attached cells were incubated at room temperature for 10 min to ensure complete adsorption. Subsequently, 50 µL of cold antibody specific to the reaction was added to each sample. The antibodies used for CUT&RUN were CDK8 (Cell signaling, 4101S, 1:50), MYC (Cell Signaling, 13987S, 1:50), RNA Pol II (Cell signaling, 2629S, 1:50), phospho-RNA Pol II (Cell Signaling, 13499S, 1:50), H3K4me1 (Abcam, ab8895, 1:50), H3K4me3 (EpiCypher, 13-0041K, 0.5 mg/ml), BRD4 (Cell signaling, 13440S, 1:50), H3K27ac (Active motif, 39133, 1:25), and IgG (EpiCypher, 13-0042K, 0.5 mg/ml). The cells were then incubated overnight on a nutator at 4°C and permeabilized using a buffer containing 5% digitonin. Next, 2.5 µL/reaction pAG-MNase (Epicypher) was added to each sample. The beads were gently resuspended by vortexing or pipetting to evenly distribute the enzymes. The mixture was incubated for 10 min at room temperature. Calcium Chloride (100 mM, 1 µL/reaction) was added to the reaction, followed by a 2-hour incubation at 4°C. After incubation, 34 µL of Stop Master Mix was added to each tube, followed by a 10-minute incubation at 37°C. The tubes were then quick-spun and placed on a magnet for slurry separation, and the clear supernatants were transferred to 8-strip tubes for DNA purification. Libraries were prepared using the NEBNext Ultra II DNA Library Prep kit and sequenced using NovaSeq PE150.
CUT&RUN-seq reads were aligned to the reference human genome hg38 using BOWTIE (v.2.3.4.1). Aligned reads were stripped of duplicate reads using Sambamba (v.0.6.8). Peaks were called using the program MACS (v2.1.2), with the narrow peak mode using matched input controls and a q-value of 0.00001. Peaks in the blacklisted genomic regions identified by the ENCODE consortium were excluded using bedtools. For downstream analysis and visualization, bamCoverage was used to generate bigwig files, and density maps were produced using IGVtools. Group 3 medulloblastoma enhancers were defined based on H3K27ac signals. Regions within 1kb of RefSeq transcription start site (TSS) locations and peaks with strong H3K4me3 signals typical of active promoters were subtracted from these signals. Annotation and visualization of the peaks were conducted using ChIPseeker (v3.18). Differentially marked genes were calculated using DiffBind and DESeq2, based on the threshold of FDR < 0.05 and fold-change ≥ 2.

Single cell RNA-seq
Single-cell RNA sequencing data were aligned against a composite reference consisting of mm10 and hg38 genomes to delineate transcripts originating from murine and human cancer cells using the Cell Ranger toolkit (version 4.0.0). The classification of cells as either human or murine was based on a threshold of 90% genome-specific reads. Cells falling below this threshold were identified as human-mouse chimeric multiplets and excluded from further analysis. Gene-barcode count matrices obtained from scRNA-seq were processed using the Seurat package (version 4.0.3) in R. Cells with fewer than 500 or more than 8000 genes were excluded to eliminate low-quality samples and potential doublets. Cells with over 10% reads mapped to mitochondrial genes were filtered out. Log-normalization was applied to the filtered datasets, followed by principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality. Utilizing Seurat’s elbow plot function, the top 25 principal components were selected for UMAP plot generation. Cell clusters were discerned via k-nearest neighbor unsupervised clustering, and the resolution parameter was set to 1.2. Established markers from literature were used to annotate each cluster with its corresponding biological cell type.

Multispectral IHC
Tumor tissues were fixed in formalin and paraffin-embedded for multispectral imaging using the Vectra 3.0 Automated Quantitative Pathology Imaging System (Perkin Elmer). Four-micron sections mounted on glass slides were sequentially stained for human CDK8 (Abcam, ab224828), MYC (Abcam, ab168727), RPS12 (Abcam, ab167428), p-4EBP1-T37/46 (Abcam, ab75831), p-S6-S235/236 (Cell Signaling, 2211S), p-AKT-S473 (Leica, NCL-L-AKT-PHOS), and DAPI using a Bond RX autostainer (Leica). Slides were dewaxed (Leica), heat-treated in ER2 (epitope retrieval solution 2) antigen retrieval buffer for 20 min at 93°C (Leica), blocked in antibody (Ab) Diluent (Perkin Elmer), incubated for 30 min with the primary antibody, 10 min with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary polymer (anti-mouse/anti-rabbit, Perkin Elmer), and 10 min with horseradish peroxidase-reactive OPAL fluorescent reagents (Perkin Elmer). Slides were washed between staining steps with Bond Wash (Leica) and stripped between each round of staining by heat treatment in antigen retrieval buffer. After the final round of staining, the slides were heat-treated in ER1 antigen retrieval buffer, stained with spectral 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (Perkin Elmer), and coverslipped with ProLong Diamond mounting media (Thermo Fisher). Whole slide scans were collected using a 10× objective lens at a resolution of 1.0 μm. Approximately 30 regions of interest were selected from the tumor in areas near the tumor border or in the center of the tumor. Regions of interest were scanned for multispectral imaging with a 20× objective lens at a resolution of 0.5 μm. Multispectral images were analyzed using inForm software version 2.3 (Perkin Elmer) to unmix adjacent fluorochromes, subtract autofluorescence, segment the tissue into tumor regions and stroma, segment the cells into nuclear, cytoplasmic, and membrane compartments, and phenotype the cells according to cell marker expression.

Animal studies
Animal care and experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the University of Colorado Center for Comparative Medicine and the University of Colorado Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol number: 00052). Mice are maintained under humidity- and temperature-controlled conditions with a light/dark cycle that is set at 12 h. All mice will be housed in cages with micro-isolator lids. Animals are fed autoclaved mouse chow and water ad libitum. Handling is performed with universal sterile precautions, and experienced personnel will perform all procedures. If an animal loses >15% of its body weight or is observed to exhibit any signs of illness (dehydration, hunched appearance, hind-limb paralysis), it will be euthanized in accordance with IACUC protocols. Mice will be euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation and decapitation. CO2 asphyxiation, followed by secondary means of euthanasia, appears to cause the least amount of distress and pain and is consistent with the recommendations of the Panel on Euthanasia of the American Veterinary Medical Association. For mice requiring cardiac puncture for blood collection, they will undergo CO2 asphyxiation first, and then a needle will be inserted under the left costal margin and aimed inward and upward until a flash is seen in the syringe; blood is then withdrawn and submitted for complete blood count.
Female athymic Nude Foxn1nu and female NOD scid (NSG, #5557) gamma mice aged 4–8 weeks were used for orthotopic xenograft studies. D425 or D458 cells were collected and resuspended in a single cell suspension of 20,000 cells/3 μl in non-FBS medium. Tumor cells were injected into the cerebellum using the following coordinates for medulloblastoma implantation: 1.500 mm mediolateral (right), −2.000 mm anteroposterior (posterior) relative to lambda, and −3.000 mm dorsoventral (depth) from the skull surface at lambda. To monitor tumor growth in D458 xenograft mice, the mice were injected intraperitoneally with 10 μl/g of 15 mg/mL D-luciferin potassium salt solution (Gold Biotechnology) and imaged using the Xenogen IVIS 200 In vivo Imaging System (PerkinElmer). Tumor bioluminescence was analyzed using the Living Image 2.60.1 software (PerkinElmer). The mice used in this study were kept in a sterile environment under 12/12-h light/dark cycle, 21–23°C and 40–60% humidity at University of Colorado, Anschutz Medial Campus, Aurora, USA. Since brain tumor burden cannot be reliably defined by size, mice were monitored daily for neurological function, body condition score, and weight loss. Animals were euthanized according to predefined humane endpoints in our approved protocol, including a maximum of 15% body weight loss.
The mice were administered a daily dose of 40 mg/kg RVU120 or 1 mg/kg TAK-228 via oral gavage. RVU120 was dissolved in water and TAK-228 was prepared by dilution in 0.5% N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone and subsequent suspension in a 0.5% polyvinylpyrrolidone solution for administration. In the combination treatment group, mice received RVU120 initially, followed by a 2-hour intermission before the administration of TAK-228. All mice were treated with the respective drugs 2-4 h before euthanasia, and blood was extracted for hematological toxicity analysis.

Immunohistochemistry
For histological analysis, tumors from experimental mice were dissected and either frozen or preserved in 10% formalin. The samples were rinsed with PBS, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde overnight at 4°C, and embedded in paraffin. Antigen retrieval was performed by the application of citrate buffer pH 6.00 for 20 min. Slides were then incubated with caspase 3 (Cell Signaling Technology, 9662) and H&E overnight at 4°C. The secondary antibody conjugated to horseradish peroxidase was detected using the Dako EnVision Kit for 3,3′-diaminobenzidine.

Flow cytometry
Cells were fixed with 4% formaldehyde for 15 min at room temperature. The fixed cells were washed and permeabilized with methanol on ice for 10 min. Cells were stained with active caspase-3 (BD Biosciences). The apoptosis was measured by eBioscienc Annexin V apoptosis detection kit FITC (Thermo Fisher). Flow cytometry analysis was performed using an Amnis FlowSight flow cytometer (Millipore).

Microarray preparation and data processing
RNA from all surgical specimens was extracted, amplified, labeled, and hybridized to Affymetrix HG-U113 plus two microarray chips (Affymetrix). The scanned microarray data were background-corrected and normalized using the RMA algorithm, resulting in log2 gene expression values. For the public microarray data, raw CEL files were downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession number GSE85217 and normalized using the RMA algorithm. The gene expression array data generated using the Affymetrix Gene 1.1 ST array and U133 Plus 2.0, array platforms were merged to generate a combined value. For each platform, the contrast value per gene was calculated by subtracting the mean expression of that gene across all samples hybridized on that platform from each individual, and the resulting contrast values of the two platforms were then combined.

Magnetic resonance imaging
For in vivo MRI acquisitions, the mice were anesthetized shortly before and during the MR session using a 1.5% isoflurane/oxygen mixture. The anesthetized mice were placed on a temperature-controlled mouse bed below a mouse head array coil and inserted into a Bruker 9.4 Tesla BioSpec MR scanner (Bruker Medical). First, T2-weighted turboRARE images were acquired using the following parameters: repetition time (TR), 3268 ms; echo time (TE), 60 ms; RARE factor, 12 and 8 averages; FOV, 20 mm; matrix size, 350 × 350; slice thickness, 700 µm; 24 sagittal and axial slices; in-plane spatial resolution, 51 µm. A diffusion-weighted EPI sequence with 6 b values was then used using four axial slices covering all tumor lesions and unaffected brain tissue. Tumor regions were manually segmented on T2-weighted images by placing hand-drawn regions of interest (ROI) and the volume was calculated in mm3. The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC; s/mm2) was calculated using diffusion-weighted imaging maps as a criterion for tumor cellularity. All acquisitions and image analyses were performed using the Bruker ParaVision NEO software (Bruker Medical).

CRISPR-Cas9 Screen
The CU Druggable Library (CUDL) consists of 9761 sgRNAs from 1140 genes targeted by 1194 FDA-approved drugs involved in metabolism, protein modifications, signal transduction, and kinases, and druggable genes of interest from multiple research labs in the University of Colorado’s Anschutz Medical Campus. The oligo pool for the sgRNA library was synthesized on a custom chip and cloned into lentiCRISPRv2 (#52961, Addgene) and lentiGUIDE-puro (#52963, Addgene). The library was transduced into D341, D425, and D458 cells in triplicate at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of ~0.3. Uninfected cells were removed with puromycin selection, and the population was cultured for a total of 18 days, after which genomic DNA was harvested, the sgRNA cassette retrieved by PCR, and the abundance of sgRNAs quantitated by Illumina sequencing. The sequencing reads were aligned to the shRNA library using Bowtie and the ambiguous reads were excluded from the analysis. Resulting read counts per sgRNA were analyzed using R-based package MAGeCK (1.10.0), which ranks sgRNAs based on P-values calculated from the negative binomial model and uses a modified robust ranking aggregation (RRA) algorithm to identify positively or negatively selected sgRNA and genes.

Study approval
All patients provided written informed consent for molecular studies of their tumors, and the study protocol was approved by the ethics committee of the University of Colorado and Children’s Hospital Colorado (COMIRBs #95–500). All animal procedures were performed in accordance with the National Research Council’s Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and approved by the University of Colorado, Anschutz Campus Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

Statistics analysis
No formal statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. Sample sizes were chosen based on established standards in the field and on our prior experience with similar experiments, and they are consistent with those used in related published studies. Samples/animals were randomly assigned to experimental groups to minimize allocation bias. Investigators were blinded to group allocation during both data collection and analysis. Statistical significance was set to p < 0.05. Transcriptomics data were analyzed using DESeq2 with an adjusted P value threshold of 0.05. R2: The Genomics Analysis and Visualization Platform (https://hgserver1.amc.nl/cgi-bin/r2/main.cgi?open_page=login) was used to delineate the association between gene expression levels and overall survival in patient samples. R package survival (v.3.2-11) and Prism GraphPad (v.10.0.2) were used for the statistics.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript presented by Wang et al. identifies CDK8 as a critical therapeutic target in MYC-driven medulloblastoma (MB), a highly aggressive brain cancer. It proposes that CDK8 regulates MYC expression, ribosome biogenesis, and protein synthesis, driving MB tumor growth. Using inhibitors like RVU120 and combining CDK8 and mTOR inhibition show potential for enhanced therapeutic efficacy in preclinical models. Although the data included in the manuscript is convincing and interesting, further experimental evidence are required to support their conclusions. I strongly believe that is important to provide much stronger evidence to determine whether CDK8 regulates protein synthesis directly or indirectly through MYC. Additionally, the authors should better discuss this aspect, considering that MYC is a direct regulator of ribosome biogenesis at multiple levels (this review provides references to excellent articles on the topic: https://doi.org/10.1038/nrc2819). Moreover, while the RNA-seq data are very robust, it would be beneficial to include an additional experiment to demonstrate the impact on rRNA transcription or its processing. In addition, throughout the manuscript, the authors should try to justify why they use shRNA, sgRNA or siRNA against CDK8 along the manuscript.
Major points:
1. In Figure 1, the authors demonstrates that CDK8 is a critical therapeutic vulnerability in MYC-driven medulloblastoma (MB). Through CRISPR-Cas9 screening, CDK8 was identified as essential for tumor growth, with its loss reducing MYC expression, cell proliferation, and neurosphere growth. High CDK8 expression correlates with poor survival in high-MYC MB, and its inhibition in mice significantly reduced tumor growth and extended survival, emphasizing its potential as a therapeutic target.
-Why in Figure 1i the authors did not validate the results by making CDK8 knock outs?. In the same figure the authors mention a “notable decrease in MYC levels” (line 2; page5), however, there doesn’t seem to be much difference between the two shCDK8 constructs, despite the differences in CDK8 depletion efficiency, especially in D425 cell line. Quantifying these levels could provide greater clarity. Validation would be more robust using one sgRNA from the CRISPR screening library and a different one as well.
-Importantly, there is no information on how the CRISPR screening was performed, which library was used, how many sgRNAs were used per gene, or how many of the CDK8 guides indicated vulnerability in MYC-driven MB tumors. This information is essential in order to publish the paper.
2. Base on the results shown in Figure 3, the authors claim that CDK8 depletion leads to significant downregulation of genes associated with mRNA translation, ribosome assembly, and protein synthesis. As far as I know, this is the first time a direct regulation of translation by CDK8 has been suggested. Important controls should be included:
- Polysome profiling in cells treated with the inhibitor (as is sown in Fig. 4g, are required). Quantifying polysomes will offer a more comprehensive and robust analysis of the impact of CDK8 depletion on the distribution between polysomes, monosomes, and individual ribosomal subunits (40S and 60S).
- Is rRNA transcription affected? EU incorporation assays would help clarify this point. The text suggests that CDK8 depletion might impact rRNA maturation, but this is not demonstrated. Specific PCR assays or northern blot should be conducted to study rRNA processing and provide evidence for this hypothesis.
- The authors suggest that CDK8 depletion might impact protein synthesis independently of MYC; however, the results are not entirely convincing, and additional experiments should be included in the manuscript. For this, I suggest to the authors to study the effect of a complete MYC depletion in cells treated with the CDK8 inhibitor or in CDK8 knockout cells, and analyze the impact in OPP, EU, rRNA processing, and survival curves.
3. Regarding Figure 4g, the authors state that the observed effect on the 80S peak "indicates that CDK8 mediates changes in ribosomal activity in MYC31 MB cells and is essential for continued ribosomal subunit assembly and overall protein synthesis." However, I do not consider this difference sufficient to support such a claim. How do the authors demonstrate a problem in ribosomal assembly? I do not see evidence of half-mers or a loss of the 60S peak relative to the 40S. Another aspect of this figure that could be helpful is performing an OPP assay on CDK8-KO cells.
- Regarding Figure 4h, why do the authors only discuss changes in 5.8S rRNA? As far as I know, this dye labels all rRNA. To support this point, a Northern blot or PCR to quantify the abundance of different rRNA fragments would be necessary.
4. In Figure 7d, the authors mention changes in p-4EBP1 but not in p-S6; however, this effect is not discussed in the text. Could the decrease in p-4EBP1 levels be independent of mTOR?. Later, with the inhibitor, both p-4EBP1 and p-S6 are affected at longer time points. What explanation do the authors provide for this observation? Additionally, what is the viability of the cells at these time points?
Minor points:
Overall, the discussion of the paper should be more extensive, including more current references on the regulation of protein synthesis through the mTOR/MYC axis, as well as explaining the role CDK8 might play in this process.

several methods and preclinical techniques providing compelling evidence for the role of CDK8 in MYC-driven
Group 3 MB maintenance and proof-of-concept data for a promising CDK8 inhibitor that can be used as a
potential treatment for this MB subgroup. Still, a few questions and concerns remain and can be summarized
here below:
Major points:
1. Authors state that MB subgroups 3 beta and 3 gamma have higher CDK8 levels, likely because of high MYC
levels. It is shown in Fig. 1g that CDK8 expression correlate with poor survival, but it is also evident that some
SHH tumors present with high CDK8 levels. Given that SHH MBs have high levels of MYCN (that shows a
mutually exclusive expression pattern as compared to MYC), it would be interesting to see if CDK8 correlates
with MYCN as well. For example, Chipumuro et al. Cell, 2014 suggests that shCDK8 reduces MYCN levels and
correlating gene expression of CDK8 with MYC and/or MYCN (in bulk or single RNA-Seq data) would be useful
and easy to include. Further, CDK8 and CDK19 would likely anti-correlate in specific subgroups of patients. Such
data is however never shown.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We agree that investigating the relationship between
CDK8/CDK19 and MYC/MYCN is important. To address this, we performed correlation analyses using the bulk
RNA-seq dataset from Cavalli et al. (Cancer Cell, 2017). These analyses revealed no significant positive
correlation between CDK8 or CDK19 expression and MYC or MYCN levels across medulloblastoma subgroups
(Fig. 3d). Loss of MYC did not alter CDK8 expression (Fig. 3f). While CDK8 expression itself does not appear to
be directly regulated by MYC, our data support the conclusion that MYC requires CDK8 to sustain the oncogenic
transcriptional program that drives tumor growth. Targeting CDK8 disrupts MYC-driven transcriptional networks.
The elevated CDK8 expression observed in MYC-high medulloblastoma is likely a consequence of the globally
hyperactive transcriptional state, rather than direct regulation by MYC. This suggests a form of non-oncogene
addiction, where tumor cells become dependent on auxiliary transcriptional regulators like CDK8 to sustain
oncogenic programs and ensure survival. We now provide a comprehensive set of data to further interpret the
relationship between CDK8 and MYC (Fig. 3) and the results section has been updated accordingly.
2. If CDK8 is low in normal cells CDK8 could be regulated by increased MYC levels in these tumors? If CDK8
itself is not amplified in patients it must be epigenetically activated or turned on by MYC. To show if MYC
regulates CDK8 levels knocking MYC out in cells would lead to decreased levels of CDK8. This would be an
important experiment that would improve the understanding of the CDK8-MYC relationship in this story.
Response: Yes, CDK8 expression is lower in normal cells compared to Group 3 medulloblastoma cells. We
performed immunofluorescence analysis comparing normal human astrocytes to G3-MB cell lines D458 and
MB002 and observed elevated CDK8 expression in the tumor cells (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Fig. 1c, d).
Additionally, MYC ChIP-seq in MB cells showed no MYC-binding peaks at the CDK8 promoter region (Fig. 3e),
and MYC knockdown did not alter CDK8 expression (Fig. 3f). Together, these results suggest that CDK8 is not
directly regulated by MYC in G3-MB.
3. RVU120 data show promising results in cell killing of Group 3 MB cell lines. Most lines have MYC amplification
or overexpression. In Fig 2b-e, apart from NHAs including a MYC low MB cell line would have been useful in
order to understand the specificity of RVU120 on MYC-driven cancers. Again, it is not clear if RVU120 would
inhibit MYC levels in these lines.
Response: We tested the IC50 values of RVU120 in low-MYC MB cell lines DAOY and ONS76 (Fig. 2b). RVU120
showed much higher IC50s in these cells, similar to those observed in normal human astrocytes, indicating that
MYC-high MB cells are more sensitive to CDK8 inhibition. To test whether MYC directly affects this sensitivity,
we transfected MYC into DAOY and ONS76 cells and observed a marked reduction in IC50 compared to the
parental cells (Fig. 4k, m). RVU120 treatment did not reduce MYC protein levels in MB cells (Supplementary Fig.
4a, b) —likely due to compensatory feedback mechanisms that promote MYC upregulation. Despite this increase
in MYC protein, RNA-seq analysis revealed that CDK8 inhibition suppresses the MYC-driven transcriptional
program (Supplementary Fig. 4c).
4. I am happy to see that more clinically relevant PDX models are included and presented in Fig. 2k. However,
why are not overall survival (OS) shown in these models after RVU120 treatment? If survival is not significant
this should be stated.
Response: This experiment was designed to examine the effects of RVU120 and to generate xenograft tissue
for single-cell RNA sequencing. We treated the mice with RVU120 for two weeks and sacrificed them on the
same day for tissue collection. Unfortunately, we were unable to obtain high-quality nuclei suitable for scRNA-
seq analysis.
5. There is no discussion of toxicity and/or side effects of knockdown, depletion or inhibition of CDK8, which
should also be very essential. For RUV120, hematology toxicity is tested which is good. Still, using RVU120 in
combination with radiation treatment or standard chemotherapy would also be both useful and convincing for
future upcoming trials.
Response: We did not observe any significant toxicity or side effects associated with CDK8 knockdown in
xenograft models. Body weight remained stable until the final few days of the study. We repeated this experiment
in a small independent cohort and similarly did not detect hematologic toxicity. Further, RVU120 has been tested
in phase 1 clinical trials in humans (NCT04021368, NCT06268574, NCT06397313) with minimal toxicity largely
limited to grade 2 GI toxicity. RVU120 is currently in phase 2 clinical trials in combination studies (NCT06191263)
and preliminary data published also show acceptable toxicity. We have clarified the discussion and included
references to these trials. We agree that combining RVU120 with radiation or standard chemotherapy could be
valuable in future studies. Our current work is focused on characterizing the effect of CDK8 inhibition in MYC-
driven Group 3 medulloblastoma and its role in protein synthesis. Investigating combination strategies is a logical
next step and indeed these studies have been initiated.
6. The CDK8 kinase is a part of the Mediator complex, which regulates gene transcription by RNA polymerase
II. Thus, it is not surprising that ribosome biogenesis genes are regulated when manipulating CDK8 levels. In
Fig 6. RVU120 shows an effect of p-Pol2. As an important comparison in several panels, other RNA Pol inhibitors
(α-amanitin or actinomycin D) could have be tested as a positive control.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. Actually, we observed that CDK8 loss led to a greater
number of significantly upregulated genes compared to downregulated ones (523 genes vs. 66 genes) (Fig. 3h).
Our data indicate that ribosomal gene expression is more dependent on CDK8 than on other cyclin-dependent
kinases involved in global transcription. For example, although CDK7 broadly regulates transcription, CDK7 loss
did not result in a comparable reduction in ribosome biogenesis–associated gene expression (Fig. 4i). These
findings highlight a more specific and essential role for CDK8 in regulating ribosomal gene transcription.
We re-evaluated total RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) and phospho-Pol II (Ser2) levels in D458 and MB002 cells
treated with RVU120 at concentrations of 500 nM, 1000 nM, and 2000 nM, and observed a decrease in phospho-
Pol II levels at 24 hours (Fig. 7f). Additionally, we performed immunoblotting on D458 and MB002 cells treated
with α-amanitin (1 μg/ml, 24 h) and found no reduction in total Pol II protein levels. Given that our study focuses
on CDK8, we did not pursue longer treatment times or higher doses of α-amanitin.
7. That mTOR inhibition is a useful targeting strategy for these tumors is well known and expected. The data on
synergy of mTOR inhibition and RVU120 is convincing. Still, RVU120 in combination with chemotherapies
(cisplatin or cyclophosphamide) or radiation therapy is never presented. Such data would be important to show,
as if they are showing good response/synergy it might be worth combining CDK8 inhibitors with standard of care.
Response: mTOR inhibition has been extensively studied across various tumor models. In medulloblastoma,
most studies have focused on the SHH subtype, with several reports demonstrating its efficacy in this context.
Several studies have evaluated the efficacy of dual PI3K–mTOR inhibitors in G3-MB. Only one study to date has
specifically evaluated mTOR inhibition specifically in G3-MB, reporting no significant effect in the D425 xenograft
model after a one-week treatment, but showing a survival benefit in the MED211 model (Rachael et al., Cancer
Letter 2021). We demonstrated that the brain-penetrant mTOR inhibitor TAK228, administered at 1.0 mg/kg via
oral gavage in 0.5% NMP and 0.5% PVP, significantly extended survival in both D425 and D458 G3-MB
xenograft models. Moreover, combining TAK228 with CDK8 inhibition further improved survival outcomes.
Notably, a clinical trial developed by us that evaluates this combination strategy (PBTC Trial C180) was recently
approved by the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium scientific committee and is in full development in collaboration
with RVYU Therapeutics. In future studies, we will further investigate whether CDK8 contributes to DNA damage
response and evaluate the potential synergy of CDK8 inhibition with radiation and chemotherapies.
Minor points
1. In Fig. 1e (and Fig. 4b) single cell data is used from MB patients. It is unclear in text and methods if this is
already published data or newly generated data.
Response: The single-cell data were obtained from our previously published study and were re-analyzed for this
manuscript. We have now revised the Results section to clarify this point.
2. Is the cohort described in Fig. 1f from Cavalli et al.? If so, this set is not properly cited.
Response: Yes. We have revised the figure legend to include the proper citation.
3. When describing how CDK8 regulate MYC levels in Fig 1i, it would be important to refer to the Fukusawa et
al. paper that already showed this relationship in other brain tumors.
Response: Thank you for the suggestion. We have now cited the study by Fukusawa et al. in the corresponding
section to acknowledge the previously reported relationship between CDK8 and MYC regulation in other brain
tumors.
4. Labeling and arrangement of panels are not optimal for Figure 1. In general, some Figure legends are not
always as informative as main text, and should be improved.
Response: Thank you for the suggestion. We have re-arranged the panels in Figure 1 to improve clarity and
readability, and we have revised the figure legend to provide more detailed and informative descriptions.
5. In Fig. 2e. to the left, the concentration of RVU120 is not indicated. In Fig 2e. to the right: no time point
indicated when the lysate was collected. That there was changes in pSTAT1/STAT1 ratio in D425, but not in
D458 is not discussed.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We have added the dose and time point information in figure legend,
as well as quantification of the immunoblot. The pSTAT1/STAT1 ratio was decreased in both D425 and D458
cell lines.
6. Related to above, number of cell lines are listed in the method section without any data, and selection of D425
and D458 as representative cell lines is not motivated; the difference in results and potential underlying genetic
causes in D425 and D458 results are not discussed.
Response: D425, D458, D341, and HDM03 are all high-MYC medulloblastoma cell lines. Additionally, we have
incorporated data from an additional Group 3 line, MB002, in several assays, including the OPP assay, shMYC
knockdown, immunoblots, and EU incorporation experiments.
7. In Fig. 2j “SEL120” instead of RUV120 is written.
Response: “SEL120” was the former name for RVU120. We have now corrected the label in the figure to ensure
consistency.
8. In Fig. 6, the results are inconsistent. Thus, I do not get to conclude that “RVU120 is more efficient” if the result
is not the same? Please clarify and modify your conclusion related to the data shown in:
Fig. 6a. decreased ppol2 and pol2 (RVU120)
Fig. 6b. increased pol2 and decreased ppol2 (shCDK2)
Fig. 6g. decreased ppol2 and pol2 (RVU120)
Fig. 6d. increased cytosolic and mitochondrial pol2
Fig. 6i. decreased cytosolic mitochondrial pol2 (RVU120)
Response: Thank you for the insightful comment. We agree that the effects of shCDK8 and RVU120 on Pol II
dynamics are not identical. The observed differences likely reflect distinct mechanisms of action between genetic
depletion and pharmacologic inhibition. Specifically, shCDK8 eliminates CDK8 protein levels, disrupting its partial
kinase activity and its scaffolding functions within the Mediator complex, which leads to Pol II pausing at
promoters and impairs the elongation of phospho-Pol II across gene bodies. In contrast, RVU120 selectively
inhibits CDK8’s kinase activity, resulting in reduced overall Pol II recruitment and decreased levels of both total
and phospho-Pol II (Ser2). We have clarified this interpretation and updated the relevant conclusions in the
Results section.
9. For many in vivo studies, information about the administration of drug(s) is missing, e.g. duration of
administration and stop points. For example, in Fig. 7 and Fig. 8: RVU120 and TAK-228 are given by daily oral
gavage. But for how long was it administrated? Does the tumor start to grow and mice start to get sick during
treatment?
Response: We initiated treatment once tumors were established, defined by a bioluminescence signal reaching
1 to 5 × 10⁵- photons, as measured by IVIS imaging. RVU120 and TAK-228 were administered daily by oral
gavage and continued until the mice reached endpoint criteria, which were defined by the development of severe
symptoms. We have now revised the manuscript to include these details regarding treatment duration and
stopping points.
10. In Methods under Compounds, please change to “CDK8 and mTOR inhibitors”.
Response: Thanks for reviewer’s suggestion. We changed it.
11. Please present more information on the lentivirus transduction protocol used and specifics of shRNA
targeting in the method section?
Response: We have cited our previous publication detailing the lentiviral transduction protocol and included the
shRNA IDs used to target CDK8 and MYC in the Methods section.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript presented by Wang et al. identifies CDK8 as a critical therapeutic target in MYC-driven
medulloblastoma (MB), a highly aggressive brain cancer. It proposes that CDK8 regulates MYC expression,
ribosome biogenesis, and protein synthesis, driving MB tumor growth. Using inhibitors like RVU120 and
combining CDK8 and mTOR inhibition show potential for enhanced therapeutic efficacy in preclinical models.
Although the data included in the manuscript is convincing and interesting, further experimental evidence are
required to support their conclusions. I strongly believe that is important to provide much stronger evidence to
determine whether CDK8 regulates protein synthesis directly or indirectly through MYC. Additionally, the authors
should better discuss this aspect, considering that MYC is a direct regulator of ribosome biogenesis at multiple
levels (this review provides references to excellent articles on the topic: https://doi.org/10.1038/nrc2819).
Moreover, while the RNA-seq data are very robust, it would be beneficial to include an additional experiment to
demonstrate the impact on rRNA transcription or its processing. In addition, throughout the manuscript, the
authors should try to justify why they use shRNA, sgRNA or siRNA against CDK8 along the manuscript.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive comments. As suggested, we have added
new data to strengthen our conclusions. Our results support the conclusion that CDK8 inhibition or depletion
disrupts ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis, and that these effects are dependent on MYC. In addition,
we now include data demonstrating that CDK8 inhibition impairs rRNA synthesis, further supporting its role in
regulating the translational machinery. We have also clarified the rationale for our use of shRNA or sgRNA to
target CDK8 at different points in the manuscript. A detailed point-by-point response to the reviewer’s comments
is provided below.
Major points:
1. In Figure 1, the authors demonstrates that CDK8 is a critical therapeutic vulnerability in MYC-driven
medulloblastoma (MB). Through CRISPR-Cas9 screening, CDK8 was identified as essential for tumor growth,
with its loss reducing MYC expression, cell proliferation, and neurosphere growth. High CDK8 expression
correlates with poor survival in high-MYC MB, and its inhibition in mice significantly reduced tumor growth and
extended survival, emphasizing its potential as a therapeutic target.
-Why in Figure 1i the authors did not validate the results by making CDK8 knock outs?. In the same figure the
authors mention a “notable decrease in MYC levels” (line 2; page5), however, there doesn’t seem to be much
difference between the two shCDK8 constructs, despite the differences in CDK8 depletion efficiency, especially
in D425 cell line. Quantifying these levels could provide greater clarity. Validation would be more robust using
one sgRNA from the CRISPR screening library and a different one as well.
-Importantly, there is no information on how the CRISPR screening was performed, which library was used, how
many sgRNAs were used per gene, or how many of the CDK8 guides indicated vulnerability in MYC-driven MB
tumors. This information is essential in order to publish the paper.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comments. In response, we re-selected CDK8 knockdown cells using
a higher dose of puromycin and performed immunoblotting and proliferation assays. The results were consistent
with those shown in Fig. 1g, h, where CDK8 knockdown significantly impaired both proliferation and neurosphere
formation. We also validated this result using CRISPR-mediated CDK8 knockout in D458 cells, where loss of
CDK8 led to reduced MYC protein levels, as confirmed by Western blot analysis. Quantification of CDK8 and
MYC protein levels has been added to the revised figure (Figure 3i, j) to clarify the observed effects. Regarding
the CRISPR-Cas9 screen, we have now included a detailed description of the screen protocol in the revised
Methods section.
2. Based on the results shown in Figure 3, the authors claim that CDK8 depletion leads to significant
downregulation of genes associated with mRNA translation, ribosome assembly, and protein synthesis. As far
as I know, this is the first time a direct regulation of translation by CDK8 has been suggested. Important controls
should be included:
- Polysome profiling in cells treated with the inhibitor (as is sown in Fig. 4g, are required). Quantifying polysomes
will offer a more comprehensive and robust analysis of the impact of CDK8 depletion on the distribution between
polysomes, monosomes, and individual ribosomal subunits (40S and 60S).
Response: We performed polysome profiling on MB cells treated with RVU120, which resulted in a reduction of
the 80S peak in monosomes. Additionally, we conducted a quantification of the ribosome profiling results, which
have been included in the revised manuscript (Fig. 5h).
- Is rRNA transcription affected? EU incorporation assays would help clarify this point. The text suggests that
CDK8 depletion might impact rRNA maturation, but this is not demonstrated. Specific PCR assays or northern
blot should be conducted to study rRNA processing and provide evidence for this hypothesis.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We performed EU incorporation assays in CDK8
knockout, CDK8 knockdown, and RVU120-treated medulloblastoma cells (Fig. 5k–m).The treatment resulted in
a reduction in EU intensity, demonstrating that CDK8 inhibition suppresses newly synthesized RNA. Since
approximately 80% of total cellular RNA is rRNA, this suggests that CDK8 inhibition also suppresses rRNA
transcription. We agree that PCR assays targeting the transcribed spacers (such as the 5’ETS, ITS1, or ITS2)
and Northern blot analysis would provide additional evidence for this hypothesis. Our current focus is on the
broader role of CDK8 in ribosome biogenesis, and we plan to further investigate the specific impact of CDK8 on
rRNA processing in future studies.
- The authors suggest that CDK8 depletion might impact protein synthesis independently of MYC; however, the
results are not entirely convincing, and additional experiments should be included in the manuscript. For this, I
suggest to the authors to study the effect of a complete MYC depletion in cells treated with the CDK8 inhibitor
or in CDK8 knockout cells, and analyze the impact in OPP, EU, rRNA processing, and survival curves.
Response: To determine whether the role of CDK8 in ribosome biogenesis is dependent on MYC, we first
performed bulk RNA-seq following MYC knockdown in Group 3 medulloblastoma cells and compared the results
to those from CDK8 knockdown. The top gene sets affected by MYC knockdown were primarily related to
mitochondrial function and ATP synthesis (Fig. 4h), whereas CDK8 knockdown/knockout predominantly
impacted gene sets involved in ribosome biogenesis and translation (Fig. 5f, g). CDK8 depletion affected a
broader set of genes associated with ribosome biogenesis and mRNA translation than MYC knockdown or
knockdown of other genes that reduce MYC levels (Fig. 4i), suggesting a distinct role for CDK8 in regulating
these processes.
We then performed OPP assays in medulloblastoma cell lines with low MYC expression (ONS76 and DAOY)
treated with various doses of RVU120. A reduction in OPP signal was observed in DAOY cells only at 4 μM
RVU120, and no reduction was seen in ONS76 cells (Fig. 4j and Supplementary Fig. 5d), in contrast to the
significant suppression observed at 0.5–1 μM in MYC-high cells. This suggests that MYC expression sensitizes
cells to CDK8 inhibition. To further test this hypothesis, we overexpressed c-MYC in ONS76 cells and repeated
the OPP assay. Upon RVU120 treatment, we observed a marked reduction in OPP signal at 4 μM, indicating
that suppression of protein synthesis by CDK8 inhibition is dependent on MYC (Fig. 4l). Additionally, the IC50 of
RVU120 in MYC-low cells with c-MYC overexpression was significantly lower compared to the parental cells
(Fig. 4k, m). Together, these results suggest that MYC enhances the sensitivity of medulloblastoma cells to
CDK8 inhibition, and that CDK8-mediated regulation of protein synthesis is dependent on MYC activity.
3. Regarding Figure 4g, the authors state that the observed effect on the 80S peak "indicates that CDK8 mediates
changes in ribosomal activity in MYC31 MB cells and is essential for continued ribosomal subunit assembly and
overall protein synthesis." However, I do not consider this difference sufficient to support such a claim. How do
the authors demonstrate a problem in ribosomal assembly? I do not see evidence of half-mers or a loss of the
60S peak relative to the 40S. Another aspect of this figure that could be helpful is performing an OPP assay on
CDK8-KO cells.
- Regarding Figure 4h, why do the authors only discuss changes in 5.8S rRNA? As far as I know, this dye labels
all rRNA. To support this point, a Northern blot or PCR to quantify the abundance of different rRNA fragments
would be necessary.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comments. We repeated polysome profiling in
medulloblastoma cells treated with RVU120 and quantified the data to clarify that CDK8 depletion or inhibition
specifically affects the 80S monosome peak. We have revised the conclusion to reflect that a reduction in the
80S peak may indicate impaired ribosome loading onto mRNAs, suggesting decreased translation initiation or a
global reduction in protein synthesis, but it does not necessarily imply a defect in ribosomal subunit assembly.
To further support CDK8’s role in translational regulation, we performed an OPP assay in CDK8 knockout cells
as well as RVU120-treated D458 and MB002 cells and observed a reduction in protein synthesis (Fig. 4d, f).
We appreciate the reviewer for pointing this out. Y10B is an anti-rRNA monoclonal antibody that primarily stains
the nucleolus and detects ribosomal RNA, specifically targeting newly synthesized pre-rRNA. The EU
incorporation assay demonstrated that CDK8 inhibition suppresses rRNA synthesis (Fig. 5k-m), supporting our
conclusion that CDK8 plays a critical role in regulating ribosome biogenesis.
4. In Figure 7d, the authors mention changes in p-4EBP1 but not in p-S6; however, this effect is not discussed
in the text. Could the decrease in p-4EBP1 levels be independent of mTOR?. Later, with the inhibitor, both p-
4EBP1 and p-S6 are affected at longer time points. What explanation do the authors provide for this observation?
Additionally, what is the viability of the cells at these time points?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. The observed decrease in p-4EBP1, but not in p-S6, in CDK8
knockdown cells may be due to incomplete depletion of CDK8. When we examined p-4EBP1 and p-S6 levels
following CDK8 knockout, we found that both were reduced (Fig. 8i). We also assessed total mTOR and
phospho-mTOR levels and did not observe significant changes (Fig. 8j), suggesting that the alterations in p-
4EBP1 and p-S6 upon CDK8 inhibition are mediated through the MYC–mTOR axis rather than through direct
regulation of mTOR itself. Additionally, we repeated these experiments in D458 and MB002 cells using dose-
and time-dependent RVU120 treatments, and observed a consistent reduction in both p-4EBP1 and p-S6 levels
(Fig. 8f, g). The delayed effects observed at longer time points may reflect a progressive disruption of MYC-
driven signaling, or an adaptive cellular response. We also assessed cell viability after 48 hours of treatment and
found that total cell numbers decreased, while the proportion of viable cells remained unchanged
(Supplementary Fig. 5c). This suggests that the observed changes are not due to nonspecific cytotoxicity, but
rather reflect a targeted regulatory effect.
Minor points:
Overall, the discussion of the paper should be more extensive, including more current references on the
regulation of protein synthesis through the mTOR/MYC axis, as well as explaining the role CDK8 might play in
this process.
Response: We agree with the reviewer. It is novel that CDK8 inhibition disrupts the MYC/mTOR axis. Within the
context of space limitations, we have expanded the Discussion and added additional references as suggested.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript by Wang et al. investigated the role of CDK8 in MYC-driven medulloblastoma, particularly
focused on Group 3 MB, which had a notably poor prognosis. Through CRISPR-Cas9 screening, the authors
identified CDK8 as a critical vulnerability in MYC-driven MB. They demonstrated that CDK8 regulated protein
synthesis through transcriptional control of ribosomal genes and showed its cooperation with MYC in driving
tumorigenesis. The study reveals that CDK8 depletion leads to decreased MYC expression, reduced protein
synthesis, and suppressed tumor growth. Furthermore, they evaluated a novel CDK8 inhibitor, RVU120, showing
its efficacy both alone and in combination with mTOR inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy.
Although there is a multitude of data of high quality, using numerous techniques, conceptual novelty is lacking.
Targeting CDK8 and mTOR signaling have already been described in medulloblastoma and other types of brain
tumors. The molecular analyses provided in this paper do employ cutting edge techniques and extensive
supporting data, but many of the current figures could indeed be supplemental and don't particularly offer new
or unpredictable insights.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. To our knowledge, and as also noted by Reviewer 2, this is
the first manuscript to describe the role of CDK8 in regulating protein synthesis in MYC-driven tumors.
1. The concept that CDK8 maintains stemness and tumorigenicity through MYC is not new, and was published
in Oncogene by the Hinoi lab in 2021.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. The referenced Oncogene paper by the Hinoi et al.
(Oncogene, 2021) focused on the role of CDK8 in maintaining stemness in glioblastoma. In contrast, our study
investigates the role of CDK8 in regulating ribosome biogenesis in MYC-driven medulloblastoma, which
represents a novel and underexplored mechanism. While CDK8’s role in stemness has been described, its link
to ribosome biogenesis and translation control in this context has not been previously reported.
2. Similarly, targeting mTOR signaling in medulloblastoma also have been described in several studies, such as
2021, Dev Cell; 2019, Sci. Rep.
Response: While previous studies have explored mTOR signaling in medulloblastoma—both focused specifically
on the SHH subgroup. In contrast, our study targets MYC-driven Group 3 medulloblastoma, which is biologically
distinct and associated with a more aggressive clinical course. Notably, only one prior study has examined mTOR
inhibitor (not dual PI3K and mTOR inhibitor) in Group 3 medulloblastoma. In that study, one week of mTOR
inhibitor treatment showed no significant effect in the D425 model, while a survival benefit was observed in the
PDX211 model (Rachael et al., Cancer Letter 2021). In our study, we demonstrate that TAK-228, formulated in
0.5% NMP and 0.5% PVP and administered daily via oral gavage, significantly prolongs survival in both D425
and D458 Group 3 medulloblastoma xenograft models. Furthermore, we provide mechanistic and therapeutic
evidence supporting the combined inhibition of CDK8 and mTOR—a combination that, to our knowledge, has
not been previously investigated in this disease context.
3. in Fig. 3, 5 and 6, some panels should be attached in the supplemental figures to make the main figures clear
and easy to follow.
Response: Thanks for the suggestion. To improve clarity and readability, we have reorganized several figures
and moved some figures to the supplementary martials.
4. As shown in fig. 1m, knockdown of CDK8 leads to dramatically reduced tumor, why the shCDK8 mice still died
40 days post tumor cells injection? In addition, the tumor cells were injected into forebrain cortex, however, the
cerebellum injection maybe more accurately mirror medulloblastoma progression.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments. While CDK8 knockdown significantly reduced
tumor growth, it did not completely eliminate tumor-initiating cells. As a result, the tumors eventually progressed,
leading to animal death approximately 40 days after injection. This is consistent with previous findings where
knockdown of essential genes—such as SOX11, BRD4, CDK7, CTNNB1, and EZH2—slowed tumor growth but
did not completely prevent progression.
We would like to clarify that the tumors were not injected into the forebrain cortex. The original text for Fig. 1m
states: “MB cells transduced with either a control shRNA (shNull) or shRNAs targeting CDK8 (shCDK8) were
implanted intracranially into immunodeficient mice”. In fact, tumor cells were injected into the cerebellum, which
more accurately models the anatomical origin of medulloblastoma. Our coordinates for medulloblastoma
injections are: 1.500 mm M/L (right) and -2.000 mm A/P (posterior) with respect to lambda and -3.000 mm D/V
(deep) with respect to the surface of the skull at lambda. We have included the specific coordinates in the
Methods. We have also included MRI images demonstrating tumor growth in the cerebellum (Fig. 1m).
5. the authors did single-cell murine cerebellar transcript analysis to check CDK8 expression pattern in different
cell types, and performed single cell analysis for G3 medulloblastoma tissues from seven patient samples. The
human cerebellum single-cell data has already been published in Nature by Northcott lab and Taylor lab in 2022.
The author may check CDK8 expression pattern in different cell types of human cerebellum.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We have attempted to access the human
cerebellum single-cell datasets published by the Northcott and Taylor labs (Nature, 2022); however, these
datasets are hosted on controlled-access cloud platforms (the European Genome-Phenome Archive and St.
Jude Cloud). As of now, we have not been granted access to either dataset. We believe our current datasets
sufficiently demonstrate that CDK8 is consistently expressed across the majority of cell populations within Group
3 medulloblastoma, supporting its relevance in this tumor subtype.
6. what do the right panel of Fig. 2e mean? There is no description for it in the main text and figure legend.
Response: The right panel of Fig. 2e shows levels of phospho-STAT1 (S727), a known direct substrate of CDK8,
following dose-dependent treatment with the CDK8 inhibitor RVU120. This panel serves to confirm that CDK8
inhibition is effective. We have added a description of this panel to clarify its purpose.
7. in fig. 1g, only 8 patients in low CDK8 group, the median cutoff mode maybe more convincible for survival
analysis.
Response: In Figure 1g, only 8 patients were included in the low CDK8 group because we selected the cutoff by
scanning p-values across different thresholds during the survival analysis. We also performed the analysis using
the median cutoff, which similarly showed that higher CDK8 expression is associated with poorer survival,
although the p-value was 0.305. This does not alter our conclusion that CDK8 is highly expressed in Group 3
medulloblastoma compared to normal tissue and that targeting CDK8 can disrupt the MYC-driven translation
program. We have now updated the corresponding figure accordingly (Fig. 3c).
8. Many sentences need to be revised. Page2 line3, “Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant
pediatric tumor” should be revised by “Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant pediatric brain
tumor”. Page2 line6, “resulting in long-term survival rates of less than 5%” should be revised by “resulting in
long-term survival rates of less than 50%”. Page9 line7-11, fig. 5d, fig. 5e, fig. 5f should be revised by fig. 6d,
fig. 6e, fig. 6f.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to detail. We have carefully reviewed the manuscript and
revised the sentences mentioned by the reviewer. Additionally, we have corrected the corresponding figure
references.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, the authors identify CDK8 as a key regulator of MYC-driven medulloblastoma, primarily
through its role in ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis. From a translational perspective, they demonstrate
that combining the CDK8 inhibitor RVU120 with the mTOR inhibitor TAK228 significantly delays tumor growth
and extends survival in MYC-driven medulloblastoma xenograft models. While the study offers valuable insights
into the mechanisms and therapeutic potential for MYC-driven medulloblastoma, several major concerns need
to be addressed before publication.
1. The identification of CDK8 in Fig. 1a-d is not clearly explained. The methods and strategies used to identify
CDK8 are difficult to understand based on the details provided in the manuscript. For example, the X-axis in Fig.
1b and 1c is not labeled.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have revised the manuscript to include additional
details describing the CRISPR-Cas9 screen and DepMap analysis used to identify CDK8. Additionally, we have
updated Figure 1 and its legend to include appropriate axis labels and improve clarity.
2. Statistical analysis should be applied to Fig. 1f and Fig.S1c.
Response: We now include statistical analyses for all relevant data. Appropriate statistical tests have been
applied, and the corresponding figure legends have been updated to reflect these changes.
3. In Fig.1g, were all subgroups of medulloblastoma (high Myc expression) considered for survival analysis?
Subgroups only should be used to do survival analysis. What is the statistical method used?
Response: In the original analysis, we used Group 3b and 3r medulloblastoma subtypes, which are characterized
by high MYC expression. In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have now included survival analyses for
the two individual Group 3 subtypes with high MYC expression (Fig. 3c). The log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test was
used for all survival analyses, and this has been added to the figure legend and Methods section.
4. In Fig 1i, stem cell makers and differentiation makers should examine whether CDK8 depletion decreased
stemness and increased differentiation.
Response: Thank you for the suggestion. We performed immunoblotting to assess stemness and differentiation
markers in cells expressing shCDK8. However, we did not observe changes in SOX2, a marker of neural
stemness, or GFAP, a marker of glial differentiation.
5. Considering the low (D425) or lack of (D458) KO efficacy of shCDK8#1 in Fig. 1i, it is unclear how CDK8 KO
significantly decreases cell confluence in Fig. 1j. Has the possibility of off-target effects been considered?
Response: To address this concern, we re-selected the shCDK8-expressing cells using a higher dose of
puromycin and repeated the proliferation assay using the Incucyte system. CDK8 knockdown resulted in a
significant reduction in medulloblastoma cell proliferation after four days. RNA-seq analysis and immunoblotting
confirmed a decrease in CDK8 levels in shCDK8 cells (Supplementary Fig. 1f and Fig. 3i). Regarding potential
off-target effects, we observed consistent changes in key gene sets, particularly those related to ribosome
biogenesis—the main focus of this study—across CDK8 knockdown, knockout, and pharmacological inhibition
conditions in multiple MB cell lines, supporting the specificity of our findings. Moreover, differences in shRNA
knockdown efficiency are likely due to their targeting of distinct regions of the mRNA, which may vary in
accessibility and susceptibility to RNA-induced silencing.
6. Which shCDK8 was used for in vivo experiments in Fig 1m and n? The sagittal images should be used to
exhibit tumor location and pathological features. CDK8 pathway should be evaluated by IHC on these tumors.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their comment. We used shCDK8 #1 (TRCN0000350344) for the in vivo
experiments shown in Figure 1, and this information has now been added to the revised Methods section. To
further validate our findings, we repeated the in vivo experiment in a small cohort (n = 3 per group), with mice
sacrificed when the control group reached endpoint criteria. Immunofluorescence staining confirmed reduced
CDK8 expression in tumors from mice injected with shCDK8-expressing D458 cells (Fig. 1l). Additionally, MRI
was performed on the same day to monitor tumor size, and sagittal images have been included to better illustrate
tumor location and size (Fig. 1m). These new data have been incorporated into the revised manuscript.
7. In Fig. 2e, the CDK8 protein level should be checked by WB.
Response: We examined CDK8 protein expression by Western blot following RVU120 treatment at various time
points and concentrations in medulloblastoma cells. We observed a transient increase in CDK8 levels at early
time points, followed by a reduction at 48 hours (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 3a, b). Since kinase activity is
commonly evaluated by assessing the phosphorylation level of direct substrates, we assessed phosphorylation
of STAT1, a known CDK8 target. As shown in Fig. 2e and 2f, phosphorylation of STAT1 decreased following
RVU120 treatment.
8. In Fig 2 j, what is SEL 120? Is it similar to the RVU120 compound?
Response: We thank the reviewer for noting the naming inconsistency. SEL120 and RVU120 refer to the same
compound. For clarity and consistency, we have updated the manuscript to use the name RVU120 throughout.
9. Why is the NHA cell line not sensitive to the CDK8 inhibitor, despite its high CDK8 levels as shown in
Supplementary Fig. 2a?
Response: The original Supplementary Fig. 2a was intended to show the localization of CDK8 and was not
exposed under identical conditions across cell lines. We re-performed immunofluorescence in NHA, D458, and
MB002 cells using two different CDK8 antibodies. These experiments confirmed that CDK8 expression is higher
in Group 3 medulloblastoma cells compared to NHA cells (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Fig. 1c, d). The new data
and corresponding figures have been added to the revised manuscript.
10. CDK8 deletion leads to a significant reduction in chromatin occupancy at promoter regions of genes
associated with other pathways, such as neurogenesis. The expression of these genes in Fig. 5h should be
further validated. Additionally, why are these genes (SMARCD3, NEFL, and RELN) considered to be involved in
neurogenesis?
Response: Thank you for the comment. We did not observe significant changes in the expression of these genes
following CDK8 depletion. However, the loss of CDK8 may create a chromatin state that is "poised for
activation"—in which genes are primed but not yet transcriptionally active, awaiting further regulatory signals.
SMARCD3, NEFL, and RELN were selected based on gene ontology analysis, which revealed enrichment in
neurogenesis-related pathways. Specifically, SMARCD3 is a chromatin remodeler involved in cellular
differentiation, including neuronal lineages; NEFL is a marker of neuronal maturation and axonal development;
and RELN is essential for neuronal migration and brain development.
11. Considering that CDK8 downregulates the mTOR signaling pathway and that mTOR and CDK8 inhibitors
have similar effects, what is the rationale for combining the two for treatment?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful question. Although CDK8 inhibition downregulates
components of the mTOR signaling pathway and both CDK8 and mTOR inhibitors show similar phenotypic
effects, our rationale for combining them is based on the potential for additive or synergistic inhibition of
overlapping yet non-identical pathways. CDK8 regulates transcriptional programs that impact upstream and
downstream effectors of mTOR, while mTOR inhibitors act more directly on translational machinery and
metabolic control. By targeting both transcriptional and post-transcriptional layers, the combination may produce
a more robust and sustained suppression of tumor growth. Our data support this by showing enhanced effects
on proliferation and protein synthesis when both inhibitors are used together. Additionally, targeting two distinct
pathways may reduce the likelihood of resistance, leading to more durable and effective therapeutic responses.
12. A concern with RVU120 treatment is its potential side effects. The authors noted that mice experienced
weight loss with RVU120 and the combination therapy, suggesting a possible cause. This could have significant
implications for its use in pediatric patients.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. RVU120 has generally been considered well-
tolerated in early-phase clinical trials, with no consistent reports of major off-target toxicities such as cardiotoxicity
or neurotoxicity. For example, RVU120 has been tested in phase 1 clinical trials in humans (NCT04021368,
NCT06268574, NCT06397313) with minimal toxicity largely limited to grade 2 GI toxicity. RVU120 is currently in
phase 2 clinical trials in combination studies (NCT06191263) and preliminary data published also so acceptable
toxicity. We have clarified the discussion and included references to these trials. These trials are ongoing, and
additional safety data will continue to emerge as dose-escalation and expansion cohort’s advance.
13. In Fig. 7f, g, and h, the authors assess the mTOR inhibitor TAK-228, which is known for its ability to penetrate
the blood-brain barrier. However, it is unclear why Torin1 was tested in the D425 and D458 cell lines in Fig. 8.
Both inhibitors should be validated in these cell lines both in vitro and in vivo for rigorous evaluation.
Response: Torin 1 is a tool compound and does not efficiently cross the blood–brain barrier (BBB), which is why
we selected TAK-228 for our in vivo studies. Torin 1 was initially used in early in vitro experiments to assess
potential synergy with RVU120 as a proof of principle in targeting these pathways. However, due to its limited
BBB permeability, we transitioned to TAK-228 for in vivo validation. In response to the reviewer’s suggestion,
we have now evaluated TAK-228 in vitro in both cell lines (Supplementary Fig. 9b, c). Additionally, we performed
additional in vivo studies using the D425 xenograft model. Treatment with TAK-228 (formulated in 0.5% NMP
and 0.5% PVP and administered daily via oral gavage) significantly extended survival in mice bearing D425
tumors (Fig. 8c). These new data have been incorporated into the revised manuscript.
14. In this paragraph, the figure labels should refer to Figure 6, not Figure 5. “Similar chromatin alterations in Pol
II and phospho-Pol II were 7 observed in both cytosolic and mitochondrial ribosomal genes following CDK8
knockdown (Fig. 5d). These chromatin changes were associated with ribosomal gene expression, as evidenced
9 by the overlap peak track of CUT&RUN and RNA-seq (Fig. 5e). The differential alterations in Pol 10 II and
phospho-Pol II peaks significantly contributed to various pathways associated with mRNA 11 translation,
including rRNA metabolic processes and ribosome biogenesis (Fig. 5f). ”
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this oversight. The figure labels in this paragraph were
incorrect. We have corrected the citations to refer to correct figure in the revised manuscript.
We thank you for your consideration of our work.
Sincerely,
Rajeev Vibhakar MD, PhD
Cancer League of Colorado Chair
Dr. Nicholas Foreman Chair in Pediatric NeuroOncology Research
Professor of Pediatrics and Neurosurgery
Morgan Adams Pediatric Brain Tumor Research Program
University of Colorado School of Medicine
Center for Cancer & Blood Disorders, Children’s Hospital Colorado
